In [[algebra]], the '''integral closure''' of an ideal <math>I</math> of a [[commutative ring]] <math>R</math>, denoted by <math>\overline{I}</math>, is the set of all elements ''r'' in <math>R</math> that are integral over <math>I</math>: that is, for each <math>i</math> there exists <math>a_i \in I^i</math> such that
:<math>r^n + a_1 r^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{n-1} r + a_n = 0.</math>
In other words, <math>r</math> is a zero of a certain kind of monic polynomial.  
This integral closure is similar to the [[integral closure]] of a subring. For example, if <math>R</math> is a domain, an element ''r'' in <math>R</math> belongs to <math>\overline{I}</math> if and only if there is a finitely generated <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math>, annihilated only by zero, such that <math>r M \subseteq I M</math>. It follows that <math>\overline{I}</math> is an ideal of <math>R</math> (in fact, the integral closure of an ideal is always an ideal; see below). <math>I</math> is said to be '''integrally closed''' if <math>I = \overline{I}</math>.

The integral closure of an ideal appears in a theorem of [[David Rees (mathematician)|Rees]] that characterizes an [[analytically unramified ring]].

== Examples ==
*In <math>\mathbb{C}[x, y]</math>, <math>x^i y^{d-i}</math> is integral over <math>(x^d, y^d)</math>. It satisfies the equation <math>r^{d} + (-x^{di} y^{d(d-i)}) = 0</math>, where <math>a_d=-x^{di}y^{d(d-i)}</math> is in the <math>d</math>th power of the ideal.
*[[Radical ideal]]s (e.g., prime ideals) are integrally closed. The intersection of integrally closed ideals is integrally closed.
*In a [[normal ring]], for any non-zerodivisor ''x'' and any ideal <math>I</math>, <math>\overline{xI} = x \overline{I}</math>. In particular, in a normal ring, a principal ideal generated by a non-zerodivisor is integrally closed.
*Let <math>R = k[X_1, \ldots, X_n]</math> be a [[polynomial ring]] over a field ''k''. An ideal <math>I</math> in <math>R</math> is called [[monomial ideal|monomial]] if it is generated by monomials; i.e., <math>X_1^{a_1} \cdots X_n^{a_n}</math>. The integral closure of a monomial ideal is monomial.

== Structure results ==
Let <math>R</math> be a ring. The [[Rees algebra]] <math>R[It] = \oplus_{n \ge 0} I^n t^n</math> can be used to compute the integral closure of an ideal. The structure result is the following: the integral closure of <math>R[It]</math> in <math>R[t]</math>, which is graded, is <math>\oplus_{n \ge 0} \overline{I^n} t^n</math>. In particular, <math>\overline{I}</math> is an ideal and <math>\overline{I} = \overline{\overline{I}}</math>; i.e., the integral closure of an ideal is integrally closed. It also follows that the integral closure of a homogeneous ideal is homogeneous.

The following type of results is called the '''Briancon–Skoda theorem''': let <math>R</math> be a regular ring and {{mvar|I}} an ideal generated by {{mvar|l}} elements. Then <math>\overline{I^{n+l}} \subset I^{n+1}</math> for any <math>n \ge 0</math>.

A theorem of Rees states: let <math>(R, m)</math> be a noetherian local ring. Assume it is [[formally equidimensional]] (i.e., the completion is equidimensional.). Then two ''m''-primary ideals <math>I \subset J</math> have the same integral closure if and only if they have the same [[multiplicity of an ideal|multiplicity]].<ref>{{harvnb|Swanson|Huneke|2006|loc=Theorem 11.3.1}}</ref>
